blocks.text: A 19-year-old is struck on the side of the head by a cricket ball, gets up, and seems fine. An hour later he becomes drowsy, then collapses with a dilated pupil on the same side. The thinnest part of the skull overlies a branch of an artery that runs in a groove on its inner surface, and a few millilitres of blood can be fatal when it collects there.

blocks.markdown: **The cranial fossae.** The floor of the cranial cavity has three steps. The **anterior cranial fossa** holds the frontal lobes, the **middle cranial fossa** the temporal lobes and pituitary, and the **posterior cranial fossa** the cerebellum, pons and medulla. Nerves and vessels pass through openings (**foramina**) in each.

rows: CN III, IV, VI, ophthalmic division of V (V1), ophthalmic veins
Middle meningeal artery, meningeal branch of V3
Glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X), accessory (XI) nerves; internal jugular vein
Medulla, vertebral arteries, spinal roots of the accessory nerve
blocks.caption: Rotundum, ovale, spinosum run in a line from anterior to posterior in the middle fossa.

blocks.title: From deficit to foramen
blocks.prompt: A tumour at the skull base causes numbness of the lower jaw and chin and weakness of chewing on the right. Which foramen is likely involved and why?

steps.text: Sensation to the lower jaw and chin, and the muscles of mastication, are supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3), which has both sensory and motor fibres.
V3 leaves the skull through the foramen ovale in the middle cranial fossa.
A lesion at or near the foramen ovale would affect V3 and produce both sensory and motor deficits.

blocks.answer: The foramen ovale (V3). Isolated numbness of the cheek would point instead to V2 at the foramen rotundum.

blocks.markdown:
**The meninges.** Three membranes cover the brain and spinal cord, from outside inwards:

- **Dura mater**: a thick fibrous membrane in two layers in the skull: an outer **periosteal layer** (lining the skull bone) and an inner **meningeal layer**. The layers are fused except where they separate to enclose the **dural venous sinuses**, and where the meningeal layer folds inward to form the **falx cerebri**, **tentorium cerebelli** and **falx cerebelli**.
- **Arachnoid mater**: a thin, avascular membrane lying against the inner surface of the dura.
- **Pia mater**: a delicate layer closely adherent to the surface of the brain and following its sulci.

The spaces are: the **extradural (epidural) space**, a **potential** space between the skull and the periosteal dura; the **subdural space**, a **potential** space between the dura and arachnoid (crossed by **bridging veins**); and the **subarachnoid space**, a **real** space between arachnoid and pia containing **CSF** and the larger cerebral arteries and veins. The **meningeal branches of the middle meningeal artery** (entering through the foramen spinosum) run between the bone and the dura, grooving the inner table of the skull at the **pterion**, the thin region where the frontal, parietal, temporal and sphenoid bones meet.

The **dural venous sinuses** drain blood from the brain: the **superior sagittal sinus** (along the upper edge of the falx), the **inferior sagittal** and **straight sinuses**, the **transverse** and **sigmoid sinuses**, leading to the **internal jugular vein**, and the **cavernous sinuses** at the side of the sella turcica. Arachnoid granulations along the superior sagittal sinus return CSF to venous blood.

blocks.title: Real versus potential spaces
blocks.text: Only the subarachnoid space exists in health. The extradural and subdural spaces open only when blood or fluid separates the layers, which is why haemorrhage can occur in them.

rows: Between skull and dura; torn middle meningeal artery after temporal bone fracture (pterion)
Biconvex (lens-shaped) clot on CT; does not cross suture lines; possible lucid interval then rapid deterioration
Between dura and arachnoid; torn bridging veins
Crescent-shaped clot crossing suture lines; common in older adults, alcohol use, anticoagulation; may be acute or chronic
Within the CSF space; commonly ruptured berry aneurysm at the circle of Willis
Sudden, severe 'thunderclap' headache, neck stiffness; blood in CSF and basal cisterns

blocks.title: Why extradural blood is lens-shaped and subdural is crescentic
blocks.prompt: Explain the CT shapes of extradural and subdural haematomas using the anatomy.

steps.text: The periosteal layer of dura is firmly attached to the skull at the sutures. Extradural blood strips the dura off the bone but is stopped at the sutures, giving a biconvex (lens) shape that does not cross them.
The subdural space has no firm attachments at sutures, but is limited by dural reflections such as the falx and tentorium.
Subdural blood therefore spreads freely over the surface of the hemisphere, crossing sutures but not the midline falx, giving a crescent.

blocks.answer: Extradural: lens-shaped, limited by sutures. Subdural: crescent-shaped, crosses sutures but not the falx.

blocks.title: Artery versus vein
blocks.text: Extradural haemorrhage is arterial (middle meningeal artery) and expands quickly. Subdural haemorrhage is venous (bridging veins) and may be slow or chronic.

items: Fractures of the anterior cranial fossa floor may tear the meninges and cause CSF leak from the nose (rhinorrhoea).
The cavernous sinus lies beside the sella turcica and contains the internal carotid artery with CN III, IV, V1, V2 and VI.
Infection of the face can spread to the cavernous sinus through valveless veins, which is why it is dangerous.

points: Foramina of the cranial fossae transmit the cranial nerves and vessels: cribriform plate (I), optic canal (II), superior orbital fissure (III, IV, V1, VI), rotundum (V2), ovale (V3), spinosum (middle meningeal artery), internal acoustic meatus (VII, VIII), jugular foramen (IX, X, XI) and hypoglossal canal (XII).
The meninges are dura, arachnoid and pia; the extradural and subdural spaces are potential spaces, the subarachnoid space contains CSF.
Extradural haemorrhage is arterial and lens-shaped; subdural haemorrhage is venous and crescentic; subarachnoid haemorrhage is usually from a ruptured aneurysm.

questions.stem: Through which opening do the olfactory nerve fibres pass from the nasal cavity to the anterior cranial fossa?

distractorRationale.a: The optic canal transmits the optic nerve.
distractorRationale.d: The foramen magnum transmits the medulla.

questions.explanation: The olfactory fibres pass through the foramina of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone, so fractures here can cause anosmia and CSF rhinorrhoea.

questions.stem: Which nerve passes through the foramen rotundum?

distractorRationale.a: V1 passes through the superior orbital fissure.
distractorRationale.c: V3 passes through the foramen ovale.
distractorRationale.d: The facial nerve passes through the internal acoustic meatus.

questions.explanation: The maxillary division (V2) of the trigeminal nerve leaves the cranial cavity through the foramen rotundum.

questions.stem: Which artery enters the cranial cavity through the foramen spinosum?

distractorRationale.a: The internal carotid enters via the carotid canal.
distractorRationale.b: The vertebral artery enters through the foramen magnum.
distractorRationale.d: The ophthalmic artery passes through the optic canal.

questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, enters through the foramen spinosum and supplies the dura and the skull.

questions.stem: Which group of cranial nerves leaves the skull through the jugular foramen?

distractorRationale.b: These pass through the superior orbital fissure.
distractorRationale.c: These pass through the internal acoustic meatus.

questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves leave through the jugular foramen together with the internal jugular vein.

questions.stem: Which is the correct order of the meninges from outermost to innermost?

distractorRationale.b: The dura is the outermost layer.
distractorRationale.d: The pia lies against the brain, inside the arachnoid.

questions.explanation: The tough dura is outermost, the arachnoid lies beneath it, and the pia is adherent to the brain surface. CSF lies between the arachnoid and pia.

questions.stem: True or false: the subdural space is a potential space containing the bridging veins.
questions.explanation: The subdural space only exists when blood or fluid separates the dura from the arachnoid. Bridging veins cross it from the cortex to the dural sinuses and can tear after head injury.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old man taking an anticoagulant had a minor fall two weeks ago and now has progressive confusion. CT shows a crescent-shaped collection over the left hemisphere crossing the suture lines. Which diagnosis and source are most likely?

options.text: Subdural haemorrhage from torn bridging veins
Extradural haemorrhage from the middle meningeal artery
Subarachnoid haemorrhage from a berry aneurysm
Intracerebral haemorrhage from the lenticulostriate arteries

questions.correctOptionText: Subdural haemorrhage from torn bridging veins

distractorRationale.a: Correct: crescentic, crossing sutures, older patient, slow onset.
distractorRationale.b: Extradural collections are lens-shaped and do not cross sutures.
distractorRationale.c: Subarachnoid blood lies in the sulci and cisterns.
distractorRationale.d: Intracerebral bleeds lie within brain tissue.

questions.explanation: A crescent-shaped collection that crosses sutures in an older anticoagulated patient with a gradual course is characteristic of subdural haemorrhage from bridging vein tears.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman has a sudden, severe headache described as the worst of her life, with neck stiffness. CT shows blood in the basal cisterns. Where is the blood located, and what is the commonest cause?

options.text: Between the dura and the skull; a torn meningeal artery
Between the arachnoid and the pia; a ruptured berry aneurysm
Between the dura and the arachnoid; torn bridging veins
Within the dural venous sinuses; venous thrombosis

questions.correctOptionText: Between the arachnoid and the pia; a ruptured berry aneurysm

distractorRationale.d: Sinus thrombosis does not give blood in the cisterns.

questions.explanation: Blood in the basal cisterns lies in the subarachnoid space, between the arachnoid and pia. The commonest cause of spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage is rupture of a berry aneurysm at the circle of Willis.

questions.stem: Compare extradural and subdural haemorrhage in terms of the anatomical space, vessel involved, CT shape and typical clinical course.
markingGuide: Extradural: between skull and periosteal dura; middle meningeal artery, often with a pterion fracture
Extradural CT: biconvex (lens) shape, limited by sutures
Extradural course: possible lucid interval then rapid deterioration
Subdural: between dura and arachnoid; bridging veins
Subdural CT: crescent shape, crosses sutures, not the falx
Subdural course: acute or chronic, commonly in elderly, alcohol use, anticoagulation
questions.explanation: The vessels and the attachments of the dura determine shape and tempo. Arterial extradural bleeding is limited by sutures and expands quickly; venous subdural bleeding spreads over the hemisphere and may evolve slowly.

questions.stem: Describe the layers of the dura and explain how the dural venous sinuses are formed and where the superior sagittal sinus drains.
markingGuide: Dura has an outer periosteal layer and an inner meningeal layer
The layers are fused except where they separate to enclose the dural venous sinuses
The meningeal layer folds to form falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli and falx cerebelli
The superior sagittal sinus runs along the upper edge of the falx cerebri
Sinuses drain via the transverse and sigmoid sinuses to the internal jugular vein
Arachnoid granulations return CSF to the sinuses
questions.explanation: Dural venous sinuses are channels between the two layers of dura, lined with endothelium and without valves. Blood drains from the superior sagittal sinus through the transverse and sigmoid sinuses to the internal jugular vein.
